sources.news_title: New Sunscreen Filter Hits U.S. Shelves As Texas Melanoma Rises
sources.text:
A sunscreen ingredient used overseas for decades is reaching American consumers for the first time as Texas is projected to record 5,910 new invasive melanoma cases in 2026.
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. renewed attention to the change, calling the arrival of bemotrizinol, also known as BEMT, “another MAHA win.” The rollout comes as federal health officials stress that sun protection remains important even as temperatures cool because ultraviolet radiation — not heat — is what damages skin.
First New Sunscreen Active In Decades
The Food and Drug Administration announced on June 9 that bemotrizinol would be added to the federal over-the-counter sunscreen monograph, making it the first new active ingredient added to the monograph since the late 1990s.
The agency said bemotrizinol protects against both ultraviolet A and ultraviolet B radiation, has low levels of absorption through the skin, and is generally recognized as safe and effective under specified conditions for adults and children 6 months and older at concentrations up to 6%.
“As promised in the Trump Administration’s MAHA Strategy Report, HHS is advancing innovation by bringing a new sunscreen ingredient to the U.S. market for the first time in 20 years. Bemotrizinol has been used safely in Europe for decades, and FDA’s action will increase competition and consumer confidence in sunscreen products.”
Kennedy made the statement in the FDA’s June release.
The final administrative order was issued June 10 and took effect August 9. The FDA explains that sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs in the United States.
Products Are Reaching U.S. Shelves
The regulatory change has now moved from agency paperwork to retail products. Neutrogena lists new U.S. facial sunscreens containing BEMT, including Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 and Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60, on its site.
Ultra Violette also launched U.S. products containing bemotrizinol, while La Roche-Posay has announced a BEMT product for the U.S. market but still describes it as forthcoming on its American page.
Cooler Texas Weather Does Not End UV Risk
The timing matters for Texans heading into cooler fall and winter weather because lower temperatures do not eliminate ultraviolet exposure.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says sun protection is important throughout the year and specifically notes that UV rays can reach people on cloudy and cool days. The agency advises using protection when the UV Index is 3 or higher.
The FDA likewise says sun safety is “always in season” and that people are exposed to ultraviolet radiation year-round regardless of the weather. Even on an overcast day, as much as 80% of the sun’s UV radiation can pass through cloud cover, according to the agency’s current guidance.
Temperature and UV intensity are not the same thing. The FDA notes that ultraviolet exposure varies with geography, altitude, time of year, time of day, weather, and reflection. The sun is generally less direct during winter, but damaging UV radiation does not disappear when the air turns cool.
That means a mild October afternoon, a cool football game, a winter walk, outdoor work, or time spent driving or sitting outside can still contribute to cumulative UV exposure if skin is unprotected.
Texas Projected To See 5,910 Melanomas
Skin cancer remains the most commonly diagnosed cancer in the United States, according to the American Cancer Society’s 2026 report.
More than 5 million basal cell and squamous cell skin cancers are diagnosed nationally each year, although the actual total is not known because those cancers are not routinely reported to central cancer registries. The CDC separately estimates that about 6.1 million adults are treated for basal and squamous cell carcinomas each year, at an annual cost of about $8.9 billion, according to its current statistics.
Melanoma accounts for a much smaller share of skin cancers but causes the large majority of skin-cancer deaths. The American Cancer Society estimates that 112,000 invasive melanomas will be diagnosed nationwide in 2026 and 8,510 people will die from the disease. Another 122,680 in situ melanomas are also projected this year.
In Texas, the American Cancer Society projects 5,910 new invasive melanoma cases and 480 melanoma deaths in 2026, according to its state-by-state estimates.
As The Dallas Express previously reported, melanoma incidence has been increasing in Texas.
Protection Requires More Than Sunscreen
Most skin cancers are caused by too much exposure to ultraviolet radiation from the sun or tanning devices, according to the CDC. The agency recommends combining several forms of protection rather than relying on sunscreen alone.
When the UV Index is 3 or higher, CDC guidance calls for seeking shade, wearing clothing that covers the arms and legs, using a wide-brimmed hat, wearing sunglasses that block UVA and UVB rays, and applying broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of at least 15.
The FDA also recommends broad-spectrum SPF 15 or higher and says sunscreen should be reapplied at least every two hours, or more often when swimming or sweating. The agency stresses that no sunscreen blocks all UV radiation.
Some medical groups recommend SPF 30 or higher for routine sun protection. The American Cancer Society advises broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher as part of a broader strategy that includes shade, protective clothing, and avoiding tanning beds.
The CDC also notes that unprotected skin can be damaged by UV radiation in as little as 15 minutes and that people can still need protection when conditions are cool or cloudy.
MAHA Strategy Targeted Sunscreen Regulation
The Trump administration’s Make America Healthy Again Strategy Report called for the FDA to promote innovation in the sunscreen market and improve the regulatory process for over-the-counter sunscreen.
Bemotrizinol became the first new active ingredient added to an OTC monograph under the streamlined administrative-order process established by the CARES Act. DSM Nutritional Products LLC submitted the request, and the FDA finalized the change after issuing a proposed order in December 2025.
The FDA’s final order also provided an 18-month exclusivity period tied to the submission for DSM Nutritional Products LLC and its licensees, assignees, or successors in interest.
The Dallas Express has previously reported on the administration’s broader MAHA strategy and its emphasis on revisiting federal health policies and regulatory processes.

sources.news_title: Sunscreens Made With Bemotrizinol Are Now Available in the U.S.
sources.text:
Sunscreens With New FDA-Approved Bemotrizinol Are Starting to Hit Shelves
“The United States has historically lagged much of the world in sunscreen chemistry,” says Melanie Palm, MD, a dermatologist and cosmetic surgeon at Art of Skin MD in Solana Beach, California. Sunscreens made with bemotrizinol have been available outside the United States for decades.
“For more than 25 years, we have been working with a fixed menu of roughly 16 approved filters, and almost every one of them is a specialist rather than a generalist. Bemotrizinol is different.”
Bemotrizinol joins just two other sunscreen ingredients that the FDA considers “generally recognized as safe and effective” (GRASE): zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. While these two ingredients are mineral sunscreens, bemotrizinol is a chemical ingredient.
What Is Bemotrizinol?
Bemotrizinol is a chemical UV filter that provides protection against UVA and UVB rays. “Most of the sunscreen options on the shelf in the U.S. only block UVB,” says Jamie Alan, PharmD, PhD, an associate professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University in East Lansing.
“While UVB is what typically causes sunburns, UVA is deep-penetrating and can drive aging and cancer. Right now, only zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or avobenzone can block UVA and UVB,” says Dr. Alan.
Bemotrizinol is a large molecule chemical, which lowers the amount of the ingredient that can be absorbed into the body, per the FDA. The larger molecule is also “not likely to impact the environment as much because it’s not taken up by plants,” Alan says.
Another benefit of bemotrizinol is that it’s photostable, which means it doesn’t easily break down in sunlight, Alan says. “Avobenzone, our main organic UVA filter, is notoriously photolabile unless carefully stabilized,” says Adam Friedman, MD, a professor and the chair of dermatology at George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences in Washington, DC.
“Bemotrizinol helps address that gap because it absorbs in both the UVB and UVA range and can also improve the stability of other filters in a formulation,” Dr. Friedman says.
Dr. Palm calls bemotrizinol “elegant and lightweight,” noting that “chemists can build broad-spectrum sunscreens that feel good on the skin — which is the single biggest determinant of whether a patient actually applies it every day.”
Evidence Supports the Safety of Bemotrizinol
A large existing body of research and real-world data support the safety of bemotrizinol.
“Based on the peer-reviewed data available, I do not have a specific safety concern that would make me hesitant about bemotrizinol,” Friedman says. “That said, ‘safe’ does not mean ‘magic.’ Safety and performance still depend on the final formulation, concentration, labeling, water resistance, patient use, and real-world reapplication.”
Bemotrizinol has also been through rigorous testing. “What makes this approval so reassuring is that bemotrizinol was not waved through on a cosmetic technicality,” Palm says.
“It went through a full FDA new-drug-caliber review under modern safety standards, supported by one of the most extensive safety dossiers ever assembled for a sunscreen ingredient: human safety studies, animal toxicology, photostability and degradation testing, pediatric relevance assessments, maximal-use absorption studies, efficacy testing, and a formal environmental assessment,” she says.
Bemotrizinol has also been reliable in other parts of the world. “This has been used in other countries for a while,” Alan says. “I have confidence in the [safety] claims.”
Dermatologists Say the Approval Is Coming at the Right Time
While regular sunscreen use has been linked to a lower risk of skin cancer, data suggests that fewer than 60 percent of American adults consistently use sunscreen.
Bemotrizinol’s features may help encourage more people to use sunscreen regularly, according to Palm. “A more capable filter that people are willing to wear consistently is, in my view, the most important kind of progress we can make in sun protection,” she says.
Overall, experts say they’re excited about bemotrizinol’s approval. “I would frame this as a meaningful advance, not a license to abandon the fundamentals: broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher, adequate amount, reapplication, shade, hats, sunglasses, and UPF clothing,” Friedman says.
“I will be buying some when it comes out,” Alan says.
Editor’s Note

sources.news_title: The First Crop of the New and Improved Sunscreen Formulas Is Finally Here
sources.text:
I’ve been spoiled. After traveling extensively to South Korea over the past few years—including living there for months at a time—I’ve grown accustomed to sunscreen formulas that spread easily and feel like second skin. Frankly, I developed a blind spot when it came to American SPF complaints. Chalky textures, greasy finishes, and white casts that leave you looking like a ghost? It all sounded a touch dramatic… until I ran out of my Korean stash.
After months of rotating through American formulas that make me want to wash my face the second I apply them, consider me humbled. Finding a Goldilocks SPF isn’t always so simple stateside—and I get why so many people are reluctant to apply sun protection daily.
Fortunately, the American sunscreen aisle is finally getting a refresh that may start to give international formulas a run for their money. It might just appease critics like me, too. In June, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) added bemotrizinol to its list of permitted sunscreen active ingredients, giving U.S. brands the chance to update their formulas with a filter that’s been used in other markets including Europe, Asia, and Australia for years. The first of the updated products are now starting to roll out—and I’m hopeful that they’ll tide me over until my next trip to Seoul.
Bemotrizinol 101 and the road to approval
Bemotrizinol (a.k.a. BEMT) is a broad-spectrum chemical filter that absorbs both UVA and UVB rays. (UVA rays contribute to premature skin aging and also play a role in skin cancer, while UVB rays are primarily responsible for sunburn.) It’s photostable, meaning it holds up well when exposed to sunlight, and pairs well with other chemical and mineral filters. Derms prize it not just for its lightweight texture but also its low potential for irritation and general suitability for those with sensitive skin, including conditions like eczema and rosacea.
While bemotrizinol isn’t guaranteed to yield a superior sunscreen—wearability ultimately comes down to the specific combination of ingredients at hand—it’s a highly regarded tool used in countless formulas that people don’t balk at applying.
And it’s been a long time coming. Manufacturers and nonprofit organizations have been trying to get bemotrizinol approved for nearly two decades, trudging uphill against an archaic system. The FDA classifies sunscreen not as a cosmetic but a drug. This requires more time and testing to get sunscreens on shelves, creating friction while limiting innovation. (For reference, the last sunscreen filter was approved way back in 1999.) We’re well behind leading beauty and grooming markets worldwide, who have far more filters to work with that drive their elegant SPF options. Bemotrizinol’s arrival doesn’t magically bring the American sunscreen industry up to speed overnight, but it does give formulators a worthy ingredient to work with.
The new sunscreens with bemotrizinol
At long last, we’re seeing some overdue SPF innovation. Following BEMT’s June approval, the first wave of formulas is starting to hit the market.
Aussie brand Ultra Violette launched its Unblock Screen SPF 50 in September, pairing bemotrizinol with zinc oxide in a mattifying formula geared for oily and acne-prone skin. Neutrogena is also early to the game with two bemotrizinol products designed for an invisible application and a cloud-like feel. The Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 is paired alongside three other chemical filters and geared for most skin types, while the Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60 includes those same chemical filters but adds niacinamide in an acne-safe formula. French drugstore favorite La Roche-Posay is also in the mix: Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 is its first bemotrizinol sunscreen for the U.S. market. The invisible, hydrating formula employs four additional chemical filters, offers 16-hour antioxidant defense, and is suitable for sensitive and acne-prone skin.
Keep an eye on this space, as more SPFs using BEMT are imminent from legacy and indie brands alike. It’s worth giving them a try—namely if you don’t wear sunscreen to begin with, have struggled to find one that you actually enjoy wearing, or are used to hoarding foreign sunscreens on your trips abroad.
The bottom line? Bemotrizinol won’t single-handedly solve American sunscreen woes, but it could help bring more comfortable, wearable formulas to shelves. This is something to embrace, especially if it’s hard to rally behind any SPFs you’ve tried in recent memory. The best sunscreens are ultimately the ones that look and feel good enough to apply daily—and you just might find that the new crop of BEMT formulas ticks both of these boxes.

sources.news_title: A new sunscreen type for Americans hits store shelves
sources.text: By — Matthew Perrone, Associated Press Matthew Perrone, Associated Press Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/a-new-sunscreen-type-for-americans-hits-store-shelves Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A new sunscreen type for Americans hits store shelves Health Oct 15, 2026 11:53 AM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that's long been a go-to option in Europe and other parts of the world. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting U.S. store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers. WATCH: Dermatologist explains benefits of newly approved sunscreen ingredient Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That's been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals. WATCH: Why sunscreen in the United States is behind the rest of the world "It's not a brand-new ingredient that you're going to be the first person to try," said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health. Here's what to know. New ingredient offers broad protection without streaks To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles. Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled "broad spectrum protection." Those that don't must carry an FDA warning label. READ MORE: Do you need SPF 30, 50 or 100? Dermatologists answer your burning sunscreen questions BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light. "This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection," said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards. A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin. READ MORE: Why it's important everyone wears sunscreen — even if you have a darker skin tone But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don't like their texture or consistency. "Those are good sunscreens," Stein said. "But for people who aren't so inclined to use them — maybe they don't like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option." There's less skin penetration with the new formula The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren't building up in the body at unsafe levels. Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was "absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood." READ MORE: How these ingredients make your sunscreen work That's not a problem with BEMT. "It's a molecule that's too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream," Stein said. "The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules." As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found. Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT "did not cause irritation" or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as "generally recognized as safe and effective," alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide. More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019. More evidence is needed about the impact on coral reefs Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs. That's led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It's estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean. The U.S. government doesn't classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like "reef safe" or "reef friendly" have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union's environmental agency has found "limited evidence of environmental toxicity" with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed. Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Those products are made with tiny particles that are more likely to be inhaled or absorbed by marine organisms. Older chemicals were often unstable Experts say BEMT has one other key advantage, in that it doesn't quickly break down in the sun. That's been a particular issue for avobenzone, the only other chemical-based ingredient that filters UVA light. "Avobenzone has been known to be particularly unstable on its own, and a lot of work and reformulation efforts have gone into trying to find ways to stabilize it," said Andrews. "BEMT is significantly more stable." As with all sunscreens, dermatologists say it's important to reapply every few hours — more frequently if you're swimming or sweating a lot. Also, people shouldn't rely on sunscreen alone when spending time outside, Stein said. Taking breaks in the shade, wearing a hat and sun-protective clothing are all important protections. "Sunscreen is just one part of an overall sun-protection plan," Stein said. "Clothing is even better." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. sources.news_title: The First New FDA-Approved Sunscreen Filter in 25 Years Is Finally on U.S. Shelves
sources.text:
The Briefing
- On June 9, 2026, the FDA approved bemotrizinol (BEMT) — the first UV filter added to the U.S. over-the-counter sunscreen monograph since 1999 — with product sales permitted starting August 9.
- Already trusted in Europe since 2000, BEMT offers broad-spectrum coverage in a single ingredient, degrades far more slowly under sunlight than most legacy U.S. filters, and leaves no white cast on any skin tone.
- Ultra Violette launched the first U.S. BEMT product on August 31, 2026; Neutrogena followed on September 17 as the first American drugstore brand, with a broader wave of reformulations expected through 2027.
American sunscreen shoppers have spent the past quarter-century choosing from the same fixed roster of UV filters every time they picked up a bottle. That era ended this fall. After the FDA approved bemotrizinol — also called BEMT — on June 9, 2026, as the first ingredient added to the over-the-counter sunscreen monograph since 1999, brands moved quickly toward commercialization. Within weeks, the first products were already reaching U.S. consumers online, and the broader market was preparing to follow.
A Quarter-Century Without a New Filter
The regulatory gap that BEMT closes stretches back to when satellite phones were a luxury and broadband internet had not yet reached most American homes. While regulators in Europe, Australia, and much of Asia approved dozens of new UV filters over the following decades, the United States treated sunscreen as an over-the-counter drug rather than the cosmetic designation used across the European Union — a classification that made the American approval process substantially slower than those of its international counterparts. BEMT had been in widespread commercial use across Europe since 2000, accumulating more than two decades of real-world safety data while American consumers had no domestic path to access it.
The logjam began to crack when Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act in 2020, which established a streamlined administrative order process for updating over-the-counter drug monographs. Under that reformed pathway, DSM-Firmenich — the Swiss-Dutch ingredient supplier that spent more than two decades and at least $18 million pursuing U.S. regulatory clearance — submitted a formal monograph order request. The FDA issued a proposed order on December 12, 2025, accepted public comments through January 26, 2026, and issued its final administrative order within approximately seven months, a pace that demonstrated what the reformed process could accomplish when applied to a well-documented ingredient.
What Sets BEMT Apart From Existing Options
Bemotrizinol is a broad-spectrum chemical filter — one ingredient that handles both UVA and UVB rays without requiring manufacturers to blend several separate compounds to achieve full-spectrum coverage. That distinction matters because the principal non-mineral UVA option currently available in U.S. formulas, avobenzone, is prone to photodegradation — it breaks down under direct sunlight at a rate that reduces its effectiveness during a day outdoors. BEMT is highly photostable, resisting that breakdown far more effectively — a property that translates into more consistent protection during extended sun exposure.
Why Deeper Skin Tones Stand to Benefit Most
Among the most persistent barriers to daily sunscreen use — particularly among people with medium to deep skin tones — has been the chalky white residue that mineral formulas containing zinc oxide leave behind. Chemical filters sidestep that problem in principle, but older options have drawn scrutiny over how readily they absorb into the bloodstream. BEMT occupies a different category: because its molecules are larger than those of most legacy chemical filters, the ingredient stays predominantly on the skin's surface rather than penetrating into the body. The FDA has classified it as generally recognized as safe and effective for adults and children as young as six months old — an age threshold that extends younger than most currently approved chemical UV filters in the United States.
Beyond the absorption science, dermatologists note that BEMT blends cleanly into the skin, leaves no visible white film, and carries a lighter sensory profile than many existing options. Researchers and clinicians widely argue that sunscreen's texture and finish are among the primary reasons daily compliance rates remain low — making the wearability of a formula a direct factor in public health outcomes, not simply a cosmetic preference.
Two Early Launches Signal What Is Coming
The first commercial BEMT product to reach U.S. consumers came from an overseas label. Ultra Violette, an Australian sunscreen brand, launched its Unblock Screen SPF 50 at Sephora on August 31, 2026 — just weeks after the FDA's final order took effect. Neutrogena became the first major American drugstore brand to follow, listing two facial formulas on Amazon on September 17, 2026: the Ultra Sheer Daily Face Sunscreen SPF 70 and the Clear Face Sunscreen SPF 60. Both products combine BEMT with the brand's Helioplex360 UV-filter technology under what Neutrogena calls its Cloud-Tech formulation — engineered for a texture the company describes as roughly 50 percent lighter on skin than its prior non-BEMT comparable formula. The Clear Face version incorporates niacinamide and vitamin E to address acne-prone skin. Broader in-store retail distribution for both products was expected to follow in October 2026.
According to Dermatology Times, those launches represent the early edge of a much larger wave of reformulations anticipated through the rest of 2026 and into 2027, as competing brands work through the manufacturing, labeling, and drug-listing requirements for incorporating the new ingredient into OTC sunscreen products.
One Supplier Controls Access — For Now
For the next year and a half, the market runs through a single source. Consumer Reports confirmed that DSM-Firmenich holds 18 months of exclusive U.S. marketing rights on BEMT, timed from the launch of the first commercial product. The company supplies the ingredient to sunscreen manufacturers under the brand name Parsol Shield. DSM-Firmenich — which first filed the ingredient with the FDA back in 2005 — has signaled its intention to monitor the exclusivity window closely and police the purity specifications built into the agency's final administrative order.
The Bigger Picture: Skin Cancer and Daily Protection
The broader stakes extend well beyond product variety. Skin cancer is the most commonly diagnosed cancer in the United States, and public health advocates have long maintained that sunscreen compliance is eroded partly by how available formulas look and feel on the skin. The American Academy of Dermatology Association called the approval "an important public health step" that expands access to effective protection and could contribute to reducing preventable skin cancer deaths. Dermatologists across multiple outlets echoed that perspective, arguing the formula's wearability advantages are not cosmetic luxuries but a meaningful lever for improving how consistently people actually use protection each day.
Clinicians are careful to frame sunscreen as one component in a broader protection strategy. Broad-spectrum products at SPF 30 or higher, reapplied every two hours, work best alongside UV-protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats, and deliberate shade. But with BEMT now available, American consumers finally have access to a filter the rest of the developed world had incorporated into everyday sun care for more than two decades.

New Ingredient Offers Broad Protection Without Streaks

sources.news_title: America's Sunscreen Gap Closes: Bemotrizinol Finally Reaches U.S. Shelves After Decades Abroad
sources.text:
Twenty-five years. That’s how long American consumers waited for a genuinely new option in chemical sunscreen protection. On October 14, 2026, shelves in Washington and stores nationwide began stocking products with bemotrizinol. The ingredient, long familiar in Europe, Japan and Korea, now carries the FDA’s blessing.
The agency finalized its addition to the over-the-counter sunscreen monograph on June 9, 2026. Fortune reported the news as products hit the market this month. This marks the first new active ingredient approved since the late 1990s. Manufacturers no longer need a full new drug application. They simply follow the monograph rules.
Bemotrizinol offers broad-spectrum coverage. It absorbs both UVA rays that accelerate aging and UVB rays that burn skin. Absorption peaks sit near 310 nanometers for UVB and 340 nanometers for UVA. Formulators gain flexibility. They pair it with existing filters to create more stable, elegant textures. No more thick white casts from mineral options alone. No rapid breakdown under sunlight that plagues some older chemicals.
Its larger molecular structure limits skin penetration. Plasma levels in testing rarely exceeded the FDA’s 0.5 ng/mL threshold. Studies reviewed by the agency involved more than 500 patients. Daily use for up to three weeks produced no irritation or allergic reactions. The FDA deemed it generally recognized as safe and effective, or GRASE, for adults and children six months and older. First time a chemical filter earned that explicit nod for young children.
Christopher Bunick, MD, PhD, associate professor of dermatology at Yale School of Medicine, welcomed the approval. “It’s a larger molecule than some of our well-known chemical absorbers to date, such as avobenzone,” he told Dermatology Times. “This larger molecule of bemotrizinol doesn’t penetrate the skin as easily, so you have less systemic absorption, potentially making it safer.”
Photostability stands out too. Testing showed 98.4% of the filter remained intact after exposure equal to 50 minimal erythemal doses. It even stabilizes companions like avobenzone. Such traits matter in real-world use. Sunscreen that survives sweat, water and hours outdoors encourages consistent application. Dermatologists have long pushed for better options precisely because many patients skip products that feel greasy or leave residue.
The path here was anything but swift. DSM Nutritional Products submitted its first request back in 2005. A new filing came in September 2024 under the streamlined process created by the 2020 CARES Act. The FDA issued a proposed order in December 2025. Public comments closed in January 2026. Final approval arrived seven months later. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. tied the decision to the Make America Healthy Again strategy. “As promised in the Trump administration’s MAHA Strategy Report, HHS is advancing innovation by bringing a new sunscreen ingredient to the U.S. market for the first time in 20 years,” he said in the agency’s release, as quoted by HCPLive.
Europe approved bemotrizinol years ago at concentrations up to 10%. The U.S. limit sits at 6%. Still, that concentration delivers meaningful protection. The ingredient carries trade names such as Parsol Shield from DSM-firmenich and Tinosorb S from BASF. DSM holds 18 months of exclusivity. Its products reached shelves first. Kenvue, parent of Neutrogena and Aveeno, confirmed plans to incorporate it. Australian brand Ultra Violette launched a zinc-bemotrizinol SPF 50 formula for acne-prone skin in partnership with Sephora, according to recent coverage in Personal Care Insights from September 2026.
Why the delay? Sunscreens fall under drug regulations in the United States, not cosmetics as in many other countries. The old monograph system moved at glacial speed. CARES Act changes aimed to fix that. This approval tests whether the new pathway works. Observers call the seven-month timeline from proposal to final order encouraging. Yet the overall lag from initial submission highlights persistent gaps between U.S. and global standards.
Public health implications stretch beyond convenience. Skin cancer rates continue climbing. Better UVA protection could reduce long-term damage. Improved cosmetic feel may boost daily adherence, especially among those who avoid sunscreen because it pills, stings or looks unnatural. Pediatric use approval matters too. Sun protection habits start early. A filter safe from six months offers dermatologists another tool for counseling parents.
Questions remain. Longer-term coral reef impact needs more study, the Associated Press noted in its October 14 report on store availability. Environmental concerns have dogged other chemical filters. Post-market surveillance will track real-world performance and any rare reactions. The FDA reviewed international safety data spanning decades. That history provided confidence. But U.S.-specific patterns could still emerge.
Experts urge perspective. No single ingredient solves every problem. Reapplication every two hours stays essential. Broad-spectrum SPF 30 or higher remains the baseline recommendation. Bemotrizinol simply expands the toolkit. It lets companies craft lighter, more stable formulas that people actually enjoy wearing.
Supply chain and manufacturing adjustments will take time. Formulators must test combinations for compatibility and efficacy. Regulatory labeling rules still apply. Consumers scanning ingredient lists will soon see “bemotrizinol” or its INCI name, bis-ethylhexyloxyphenol methoxyphenyl triazine, alongside familiar actives.
The arrival feels overdue to many in dermatology. “This is historic,” Jane Yoo, MD, assistant clinical professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told one industry outlet. No streaks: Sunscreen ingredient used in Europe for 25 years now available in US
Americans can now purchase a newly approved sunscreen ingredient that has been popular in Europe since the 20th century as Neutrogena and other manufacturers release their first products in the U.S. containing bemotrizinol.
Big picture view:
Bemotrizinol, which is also known as BEMT, is designed to shield users from both ultraviolet A and B rays without leaving those white streaks caused by mineral-based sunscreens. The products are arriving on store shelves after the Food and Drug Administration approved the chemical earlier this year.
The backstory:
In June, the FDA signed off on the ingredient, saying it met the agency’s standards for protecting people from the sun’s harmful rays without too much being absorbed through the skin. It is approved for children who are 6 months and older and adults.

Benefits of bemotrizinol
The FDA requires all sunscreens to protect against UVA, which poses higher risks of cancer and wrinkles, and UVB, which is to blame for most sunburns. WASHINGTON — For the first time in more than a quarter-century, Americans have a new option when shopping for sunscreen: a skin-protecting chemical that’s long been a go-to option in Europe and other parts of the world, AP reported.
The US Food and Drug Administration approved bemotrizinol — sometimes called BEMT — in June. The first sunscreens containing it are now hitting US store shelves, including formulas from Neutrogena and other manufacturers.
Dermatologists say the chemical fills an important market gap by offering broad protection, like the most well-established sunscreen ingredients, but without their cosmetic downsides, including white streaking.
BEMT has decades of safety data behind it, including studies showing it has minimal absorption into the skin. That’s been a concern with some older sun-blocking chemicals.
“It’s not a brand-new ingredient that you’re going to be the first person to try,” said Dr. Jennifer Stein, a dermatologist at NYU Langone Health.
To be effective, sunscreens must protect against both forms of ultraviolet light that can damage the skin — UVB rays, which cause most sunburn, and UVA rays that pose the greatest risk of skin cancer and wrinkles.
Sunscreens that block both forms are labeled “broad spectrum protection.” Those that don’t must carry an FDA warning label.
BEMT is the first chemical-based sunscreen in the U.S. that offers this dual protection. Previously, manufacturers had to mix multiple ingredients to protect against both UVA and UVB light.
“This ingredient provides a solution for what is currently a big gap with respect to providing strong UVA protection,” said David Andrews, chief science officer of the Environmental Working Group, a nonprofit that advocates for higher sunscreen standards.
A different class of sunscreens, using minerals such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, has long been shown to offer strong protection against both forms of ultraviolet light. These mineral-based formulas work by physically blocking harmful rays from the skin.
But some people — particularly those with darker complexions — tend to avoid them because they cause white streaking and discoloration. In other cases, people don’t like their texture or consistency.
“Those are good sunscreens,” Stein said. “But for people who aren’t so inclined to use them — maybe they don’t like how it feels on their skin — this is a nice option.”
The fact that chemical-based sunscreens are absorbed into the skin means they have to be carefully studied to make sure they aren’t building up in the body at unsafe levels.
Last month, the FDA revoked approval of an older chemical ingredient, oxybenzone, after determining it was “absorbed through the skin to a greater extent than previously understood.”
“It’s a molecule that’s too big to really penetrate through the skin and get absorbed into the bloodstream,” Stein said. “The older chemical sunscreens had small molecules.”
As part of its safety review, the FDA reviewed studies of BEMT in more than 500 patients conducted by Dutch manufacturer DSM Nutritional Products. Levels of the chemical absorbed into the skin were nearly undetectable, the studies found.
Agency reviewers said research in people who used the sunscreen daily for up to three weeks showed that BEMT “did not cause irritation” or allergic reactions. As a result, the FDA designated the ingredient as “generally recognized as safe and effective,” alongside the older mineral ingredients zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.
More than a dozen other ingredients are currently used in U.S. sunscreens, but the FDA has said they will require additional evidence to support their safety and effectiveness. The FDA review is part of an ongoing effort to overhaul U.S. sunscreen ingredients that kicked off in 2019.
Scientists have shown that some sunscreen ingredients can trigger bleaching and damage coral reefs. That’s led to bans on two chemical ingredients — oxybenzone, the ingredient recently targeted by the FDA, and octinoxate — in Hawaii and parts of Florida. It’s estimated about 25% of the sunscreen people apply to their skin washes off while swimming or wading in the ocean.
The U.S. government doesn’t classify the environmental impact of sunscreens, and marketing claims like “reef safe” or “reef friendly” have no standard definition or requirements. The European Union’s environmental agency has found “limited evidence of environmental toxicity” with BEMT, but longer-term research is needed.
Mineral ingredients like zinc oxide are generally considered safer for the environment, although some experts recommend staying away from so-called nano formulations. Those products are made with tiny particles that are more likely to be inhaled or absorbed by marine organisms.
Experts say BEMT has one other key advantage, in that it doesn’t quickly break down in the sun. That’s been a particular issue for avobenzone, the only other chemical-based ingredient that filters UVA light.
“Avobenzone has been known to be particularly unstable on its own, and a lot of work and reformulation efforts have gone into trying to find ways to stabilize it,” said Andrews. “BEMT is significantly more stable.”
As with all sunscreens, dermatologists say it’s important to reapply every few hours — more frequently if you’re swimming or sweating a lot.
Also, people shouldn’t rely on sunscreen alone when spending time outside, Stein said. Taking breaks in the shade, wearing a hat and sun-protective clothing are all important protections.
“Sunscreen is just one part of an overall sun-protection plan,” Stein said. “Clothing is even better.”
